explanations.explanation: Paul, who is writing this letter, opens with "…a prisoner of Christ Jesus…" Before he asks for anything, he tells Philemon right where he's sitting. I think that sets a humble tone for everything that follows. Nobody gets a more honest introduction than that.

explanations.answer: A servant of the church in Rome
explanations.explanation: Paul's opening line doesn't name a church or a city. He calls himself "…a prisoner of Christ Jesus…" (Philemon 1:1). That's the whole introduction. He's not listing a job title, friend, he's telling Philemon where he is.

explanations.answer: A shepherd of the flock in Ephesus
explanations.explanation: Shepherd is a nice picture, but it isn't in this verse. Paul says he's "…a prisoner of Christ Jesus…" with no flock and no town named. He's writing from chains, not from a pasture. My mustache can wave a lot of things around, but it can't turn that into a sheep job.
Verse 2 says "…the church that meets at your house…" That means Philemon's house. Believers gathered at home. I hope Philemon owned enough chairs, friend.
A synagogue isn't mentioned in this letter. Paul writes to "…the church that meets at your house…" (Philemon 1:2). So the meeting place is Philemon's home. That's a church at a house.

There's no river in this letter. Paul says the church is "…the church that meets at your house…" (Philemon 1:2). That puts the meeting at Philemon's home, under a roof. Good news for anybody who hates sand in their shoes.
Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers…" Always is a big word. It means Philemon comes up in Paul's prayers over and over.
That's right, friend. Paul writes, "I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers…" Not once in a while, ALWAYS. Imagine being the person somebody never stops thanking God for.

explanations.answer: His faith in Jesus and love for the saints
explanations.explanation: Paul says he hears about "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." That's the news that reaches him. Faith toward Jesus and love toward God's people, side by side. Good news travels, friend, even to a man in chains.

explanations.answer: His big gifts to the poor and the widows
explanations.explanation: Gifts to the poor and the widows aren't what Paul mentions here. He says he hears about "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." (Philemon 1:5). Two items on the list, and neither one is a donation receipt.

explanations.answer: His bold preaching in the towns nearby
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention preaching in this verse. What he hears about is "…your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints." (Philemon 1:5). Faith and love, that's the report. No towns, no sermons, just those two.

Paul says, "…you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints." The saints are God's people, and Philemon's love has lifted them. Paul calls him brother right there, too. I bet that sentence made Philemon smile.
Paul says it plainly: "…you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints." So the statement is true. Philemon's love lifted God's people. Paul even calls him brother while he says it.

Paul writes, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love." He's just said he's bold enough to order Philemon, and then he sets that aside. He picks the gentler road on purpose. A man with a strong hand choosing a soft ask, friend, that's something.
Insist is close in feeling to ordering, and that's the road Paul leaves alone. In verse 9 he says, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love." The word is appeal, and love is the basis.
Paul doesn't say decide. He says, "I prefer to appeal on the basis of love." He isn't making the choice for Philemon, he's asking him. The word is appeal, and love is the reason.

Paul says Onesimus is his child, "…whose father I became while I was in chains." Onesimus is the man Paul is appealing for in this letter. So Paul's chains didn't stop something good from happening. Paul calls him his child, and that's a lot of love packed into one word.

Paul did make tents (Acts 18:3), but that's not what this verse says. He says he became Onesimus's father "…while I was in chains." Onesimus is the man Paul is appealing for. The chains are the setting, not a tent shop.

explanations.answer: While he was out at sea
explanations.explanation: There's no ship in this letter, friend. Paul says he became Onesimus's father "…while I was in chains." Onesimus is the man Paul is appealing for. So the answer is chains, not waves.

explanations.answer: He was useless and now he's useful
explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me." He says it to Philemon and about himself too. Both of them benefit now. That's quite the turnaround for one man.

explanations.answer: He was sick and now he's healthy
explanations.explanation: Sickness isn't part of this letter. Paul says, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me." (Philemon 1:11). The change is from useless to useful. Sick to healthy isn't the move Paul describes.

explanations.answer: He was poor and now he's wealthy
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse talks about money. Paul says, "Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me." (Philemon 1:11). The change is useless to useful. Nobody's counting coins, friend.
Paul says the opposite. He writes, "I would have liked to keep him with me…" He even says why: so Onesimus could minister to him in his chains for the gospel. So Paul did want him around.

That's right. Paul writes, "I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel." He wanted Onesimus close. And he sends him back anyway.

explanations.answer: So Philemon's goodness comes by free will
explanations.explanation: Paul says he didn't want to act without consent "…so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will." He wants Philemon's good deed to be Philemon's own. I think that's why he asks instead of orders. A gift tastes better when nobody twisted your arm, friend.

explanations.answer: So the church can settle it all together
explanations.explanation: The church settling it together isn't Paul's reason here. He says he didn't want to act without consent "…so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will." (Philemon 1:14). The choice is Philemon's. Paul wants it to come from him.

explanations.answer: So the authorities won't punish Paul for it
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any authorities in this verse. The reason he gives is "…so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will." (Philemon 1:14). It's about Philemon's freedom to choose. That's all the text says.
Paul says Onesimus was separated "…so that you might have him back for good…" For good means for keeps, friend. Paul only says perhaps, so he's offering a way to see it, not announcing a fact.
Paul doesn't say a season. The verse says "…so that you might have him back for good…" That's the whole phrase. Not for a while, but for good.
Paul doesn't put a number on it. He says "…so that you might have him back for good…" (Philemon 1:15). That means for keeps, not for a set time. No calendar needed, friend.

Paul says "…no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." That's a big change in how Philemon might see Onesimus. And Paul adds that he's beloved to Philemon both in person and in the Lord. A brother is family, friend.

A servant is close to what Paul is moving away from. He says "…no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." (Philemon 1:16). The word is brother. That's what Paul is asking Philemon to see.

Paul does talk about a guest room later, but not here. In this verse he says "…no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." (Philemon 1:16). The word is brother. Not a guest, family.

Paul writes, "So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me." That's a big ask, and he's tying it to their friendship. Whatever welcome Philemon would give Paul, Paul asks him to give Onesimus. He's not mentioning that lightly, friend.

That statement matches what Paul says. He writes, "So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me." So the answer is True. Paul asks that Onesimus get the welcome Paul would get.

Paul says, "But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account." He's offering to cover it if there's anything owed. I think that's a lot of love for one letter. A man in chains offering to pay the tab if there is one.
Paul doesn't say friends. He writes, "…charge it to my account." (Philemon 1:18). If Onesimus owes anything, Paul offers to cover it himself. He's not passing the bill around.
Paul doesn't send the bill to the church. He writes, "…charge it to my account." (Philemon 1:18). If there's anything owed, Paul offers to put it on his own account. He steps up himself.

Paul writes, "Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ." Earlier he said Philemon refreshed the hearts of the saints. Now he asks for the same refreshing for himself. Even a man in chains likes a little encouragement, friend.
Paul really does ask this. He writes, "Refresh my heart in Christ." That's the same kind of refreshing he said Philemon gave the saints in verse 7. So the statement is true.

Paul writes, "Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask." He's not just hoping for the minimum. He expects Philemon to go beyond what he asked. That's a big vote of confidence, friend.

explanations.answer: Only part of what Paul asks
explanations.explanation: Paul expects far more than part. He writes, "…knowing that you will do even more than I ask." (Philemon 1:21). That's confidence, not doubt. He thinks Philemon will go past the request.
The church doesn't come up in this verse. Paul says, "…knowing that you will do even more than I ask." (Philemon 1:21). His trust is in Philemon himself. And he expects more, not less.

explanations.answer: His fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" That's the title the text gives him. Paul passes his greetings along so Philemon hears from him. I think a hello from a fellow prisoner means a lot.

explanations.answer: His messenger to all the churches
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't call Epaphras a messenger here. He says, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" (Philemon 1:23). Epaphras is the one Paul calls his fellow prisoner. That's the title the text gives him.

explanations.answer: His host for the whole journey
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't call Epaphras a host. He says, "Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings…" (Philemon 1:23). Paul calls him his fellow prisoner. No journey is mentioned here, friend.
